title: Strong markets. A divided consumer.
deck: My read after Friday’s close: the equity rebound and weak household sentiment are not mutually exclusive. Delta’s results offer a company-level counterweight to survey pessimism, but profitability depends on costs as well as demand. For valuation work, ask which customers a business serves before applying one economy-wide growth assumption.

sections.title: Friday’s rebound did not erase the weekly split.
sections.body: AP reported Friday gains of 0.8% for the Dow, 0.6% for the Nasdaq Composite and 0.5% for the Russell 2000. Across the week, the S&P 500 gained 1.2% while the Russell lost 0.9%. Treasury’s two-year par yield rose five basis points to 4.80%, ten years rose two to 5.24%, and thirty years stayed at 5.60%. My interpretation: the rebound was not simply a response to cheaper Treasury financing. Small caps participated on Friday but still lagged over the week. That is a useful caution against extrapolating one strong day, not proof of a recession or a specific cause of the rally.

sections.title: Present conditions weakened; expectations did not move together.
sections.body: Michigan’s preliminary October survey put current conditions at 44.7 versus 50.9 in September, while its expectations index rose to 47.3 from 46.3. Year-ahead inflation expectations edged up to 4.7% from 4.6%. My assessment: the composition matters more than calling every component a deterioration. The survey described particular weakness among lower-income households and those with smaller stock portfolios. That supports testing differences between customer groups, but sentiment is not observed expenditure and inflation expectations are not realized inflation. A counterargument is that pessimistic consumers may continue spending if employment and income hold up. Actual volumes and margins are the necessary cross-check.

sections.title: Delta shows why demand and profitability need separate tests.
sections.body: Delta’s September-quarter release reported GAAP operating revenue of $20.2 billion and a 7.2% operating margin. Its adjusted presentation showed $17.6 billion of revenue and a 9.4% margin; GAAP earnings per share were $1.15 versus adjusted EPS of $1.72. These are different reporting bases, not interchangeable results. Management described strong travel demand. My inference: this is a counterexample to treating weak sentiment as evidence that all discretionary spending has collapsed. It is not proof that all households or airlines are equally resilient. Reported operating cash flow was $1.7 billion; that is not free cash flow available after capital investment. Costs and reinvestment remain essential to the valuation.

sections.title: Model the customer, then the cash.
sections.body: For a consumer-facing business, build a lower-growth case tied to its customer mix rather than mechanically applying a sentiment-index change to revenue. In the LBO Deal Lab, vary revenue growth and EBITDA margin separately, holding the exit multiple fixed to isolate the effect on debt repayment. In the DCF, begin with normalized unlevered free cash flow—not adjusted EPS or reported operating cash flow. An airline additionally needs careful treatment of fleet investment, leases and seasonality; the toolkit is a simplified scenario tool, not a complete Delta valuation. Broad-based spending strength and stable cash margins would challenge the cautious case; weaker volumes despite price increases would reinforce it.

watch: Check whether small-company participation persists beyond Friday and closes the weekly gap with large-company indexes.
Compare future spending and earnings releases with the survey’s split between current conditions and expectations; watch customer volumes, not revenue alone.
Reconcile GAAP and adjusted results, then capital spending and lease obligations, before turning an earnings headline into a free-cash-flow forecast.
caveat: Codex’s analysis, not Owen’s personal view or investment advice. Research completed at the actual ET/HKT cutoff above, later than the scheduled run. Equity closes and Treasury observations cover 9 October, the latest completed US cash session. Michigan’s October figures are preliminary survey results released on 9 October, not realized spending or inflation. Delta’s release on the same date covers its September quarter; its adjusted figures are non-GAAP. Treasury data are daily par yields, not executable quotes or corporate borrowing rates. Equity percentage changes are rounded. These sources measure different populations and periods. Interpretations are conditional, not demonstrated explanations of daily market moves. Calculator scenarios are educational.
